summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.executive_summary: Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries because they promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs relative to liquid electrolytes. Among candidates, cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) stands out for its excellent interfacial stability against metallic Li, but it is not stable at room temperature and is typically stabilised with substitutional dopants on the 24d sites. c-LLZO crystallises in the Ia 3d space group with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites, and there is no consensus on the correct Li occupancy ratio. Prior computational studies have relied on a single experimental occupancy as a starting point to build an idealised unit cell, which raises the concern that predicted structures may not be near the ground state and that derived thermodynamic and observable properties may be poorly described. This study introduces a combinatorial workflow that generates all possible Li site occupancies for a c-LLZO unit cell and orders them energetically. The authors first eliminate structures with overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å, then remove symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to reduce the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10 8 structures to ~2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model trained on 1235 single-point DFT calculations performed with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) to energetically rank the remaining structures. The workflow finds that all structures occur within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure, that 19 of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a 24d:96h ratio of 8:48, and that four structures within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the ground state share the same 24d configuration with only slight variations in the 96h configuration. The authors argue that a large proportion of previously reported experimental and theoretical structures may not be physically feasible or stable, and they provide all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and does not report a formal bibliography, so top_influential_citations is empty. Notable omissions include the absence of author affiliations, participant demographics (not applicable to a computational study), and detailed hyperparameter reporting beyond the DFT settings.

Executive Summary
Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries because they promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs relative to liquid electrolytes. Among candidates, cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) stands out for its excellent interfacial stability against metallic Li, but it is not stable at room temperature and is typically stabilised with substitutional dopants on the 24d sites. c-LLZO crystallises in the Ia 3d space group with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites, and there is no consensus on the correct Li occupancy ratio. This study introduces a combinatorial workflow that generates all possible Li site occupancies for a c-LLZO unit cell and orders them energetically. The authors first eliminate structures with overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å, then remove symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to reduce the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10 8 structures to ~2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model trained on 1235 single-point DFT calculations performed with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) to energetically rank the remaining structures. The workflow finds that all structures occur within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure, that 19 of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a 24d:96h ratio of 8:48, and that four structures within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the ground state share the same 24d configuration with only slight variations in the 96h configuration. The authors argue that a large proportion of previously reported experimental and theoretical structures may not be physically feasible or stable, and they provide all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and does not report a formal bibliography, so top_influential_citations is empty. Notable omissions include the absence of author affiliations, participant demographics (not applicable to a computational study), and detailed hyperparameter reporting beyond the DFT settings.

Research Context
The motivation is that solid electrolytes offer higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs versus liquid electrolytes. c-LLZO has the best interfacial stability of all popular fast ion conducting solid electrolytes against metallic Li. c-LLZO has two primary polymorphs, the highly conducting disordered cubic LLZO (c-LLZO) and ordered tetragonal LLZO (t-LLZO).

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central problem is that experimental and theoretical works have been unable to uncover the ground state configuration of c-LLZO.

Methodological Details
The study targets the crystallographically predicted structure of c-LLZO with a Hermann-Maguin space group of Ia 3d. c-LLZO has Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites, which the authors use as the framework for generation. The authors neglect to include the 48g site that occurs between the 96h sites as it is not reported in most refinements. The total number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is 120 56 ≈ 7.4 × 10 34, rendering brute-force combinatorial search unviable. The authors eliminate overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å. The chosen cutoff of 1.7 Å is less than 2 times the ionic radius of a Li atom and smaller than the minimum distance in t-LLZO (2.56 Å). Any minimal distance between 1.67 Å and 2.3 Å would be suitable for a numerical implementation. The geometric constraint limits 96h occupancy because each 96h site exists as a pair within 0.68 Å of each other. Each 24d occupation eliminates 4 out of 96h sites as they are within 1.67 Å of this site. The authors generate all possible structures using the crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors generate all allowed structures by first generating all possible 24d permutations for a given 24d occupancy. The authors then populate the remaining 96h sites such that no two nearest neighbours are occupied simultaneously. The generation produces approximately 2.3 × 10 8 structures, including symmetry-equivalent duplicates. The authors construct the upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice for each structure. The connectivity matrix is defined as the distances between each Li atom to every other Li atom. The matrix is then flattened and sorted to ensure uniformity in all matrices. The authors use local sensitive hashing (LSH) to perform fast approximate similarity searches. The use of LSH optimises the pairwise comparison from scaling at O(N 2 ) to O(N ). The symmetry comparison method allows symmetry checks on over 100 million structures in a reasonable time frame. Only approximately 1% of structures are symmetrically unique, allowing a reduction by a further factor of approximately 100. The reduced configuration space is around 2 × 10 6 structures, which the authors then energetically order. The authors perform DFT calculations on small subsets to fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model.

Key Results
The authors performed 1235 single point DFT calculations in total. The DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code, which scales linearly with the number of atoms. The authors used the PBE GGA exchange correlation functional with a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV. The authors used a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV. The structures were represented by a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions. The data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio. The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. All structures are found to occur within a range of 5.8 eV of our lowest energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48, with the 19th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground state structures. There are four structures, all 8:48, within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest energy structure. The COMPASSIII forcefield ordered the 13:43 ratio with a correlation coefficient of 0.991.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation is indicated by the average energy for each ratio increasing with increasing 24d occupancy. The four lowest energy structures have very similar atomic coordinates with only slight variations in the 96h configuration. The authors note that the energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. The geometry optimisation results indicate that movement from original sites is preferable to attain lower energies. The authors conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature predicts structures not reflective of a real system.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors acknowledge that the energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. The authors assume a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which is an approximation. The authors have tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. A large-scale energy prediction of the geometry optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication. The authors note that the Coulombic forces alone are not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures. The authors acknowledge that the trade-off for increased speed and lower memory costs is the high specificity of the LSH method. The authors acknowledge that the COMPASSIII issue was considered too large to surmount in this paper. The authors neglect to include the 48g site, which may limit the completeness of the generated structures. The paper is a preprint not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv, which may limit its reliability.

Claims
A combinatorial workflow can generate and energetically order all crystallographically predicted structures for crystals with partially occupied sites. The workflow generates all allowed structures and orders them energetically. The authors created a fast evaluation procedure to generate and energetically order all crystallographically predicted structures. The authors acknowledge that the energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. The authors acknowledge that the Coulombic forces alone are not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. The authors provide all structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility.

Data And Code Availability
The authors provide all structures generated in a freely accessible database. The authors provide both scripts for the symmetry checking methodology in the SI section. The authors provide all input files in SI sections. The authors provide the data for Figure 1 in the supporting information (Tables S1 and S2 ).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors validated the symmetry checking methodology against more rigorous methods using the two smallest 24d:96h ratios. The authors validated the method for both 13:43 and 12:44 ratios. The authors found that including the symmetry of the structure in the MLR model made a negligible difference. The authors tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. The authors performed 20 geometry optimisation calculations to assess the effect of geometry relaxed structures. The authors found that none of the site changes correlated significantly with the geometry optimised energy.

Ethical Considerations
The paper is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. The paper is a preprint not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the 24d:96h ratios that cannot exist without a Li-Li interaction below the crystal ionic diameter. Figure 2b shows that 19 of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. Figure 3 shows the workflow to find the 4 final structures from given occupancies. Figure S4 shows the energy of a Li Dimer with changing inter-atomic distance. Figure S5 shows MLR energies compared to the order of the individual structure space group. Table S1 reports all experimental papers that explicitly report the site occupancies of the 24d and 96h sites. Table S2 reports all theoretical studies that explicitly report their 24d:96h ratio.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a workflow to generate and energetically order all crystallographically predicted structures for crystals with partially occupied sites. 2. The strongest evidence is the MLR model achieving a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. 3. The future path is to extend the method to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.
